_readme: The one way this project writes a date or a time for a person to read.
There are two implementations and there have to be: the dashboard
formats in the browser, and the mothman CLI formats in Python. Neither
suite owns this table - tests-js/display-time.test.js and
tests/test_display_time.py both read it - so neither side can quietly
bend a case to whatever it already does.
The same shape as status-cases.json, and for the same reason: two
implementations of one rule drifted once already (plans/qa-pipeline.md
item 74) and the drift rendered a check with 14 real violations GREEN.
Every `at` below is an ISO-8601 instant WITH its offset, which is how
every instant in this project is stored (criterion 10 - this standard
changes nothing about storage). The expected strings are what a person

_why: One date string with an optional time in front of it, rather than two
formats. Keith's two dictated examples disagreed on the comma, and the
cheapest way to settle that is not to pick a winner but to stop having
two strings - so there is no rule about when the comma appears,
because it always does, in the same place.
No timezone label anywhere, because there is only one: everything a
person reads is on the asset's own clock (criteria 5 and 6).

day_cases.why: Weekday, day, month, year - the form Keith dictated.
Keith's own call - always, not only when it is not the current year. The narrower reading needs a rule and can surprise a reader.

Criterion 5. 6:30pm UTC is 2:30am the NEXT DAY in Perth. This is the whole bug - every date on the page rendered in the viewer's zone, so a reader west of UTC saw the previous day with no indication anything had been re-interpreted.
The same moment as the case above, written with its real offset.

instant_cases.why: The time prefixed onto the same date string - not a second format.
Criterion 3. Lowercase, no full stops, no leading zero on the hour.
Criterion 3, and the reason is alignment - a column of times where some have minutes and some do not does not line up.
Not 0:00am. The twelve-hour clock's own two awkward cases are pinned rather than left to each implementation.
Criterion 5 again, with the time. A supply that arrived at 2:30am Perth must not read as 6:30pm the previous day.
Criterion 7. This exact shape - 43 of them - was landing RAW in the supply-history table's timing column.

relative_cases._why: Criterion 11. Both directions, scaling by unit, and never falling back to an absolute date at any threshold.
